Content:
If we have a trigonometric equation like

Content:
[MATH: \cos \theta = \dfrac{1}{2}]

Content:
and we want to solve for [MATH: \theta,] we can apply the corresponding inverse trigonometric function to both sides of the equation to "cancel" out the trigonometric function.

Content:
Here, the trigonometric function is [MATH: \cos,] so the inverse trigonometric function is [MATH: \arccos,] and we have

Content:
[MATH: \arccos (\cos θ)|= \arccos ((1)/(2)); θ|= 60^{∘}.]

items.title: Calculating Unknown Angles Using Inverse Trigonometric Functions

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: \cos\theta=0.64] and [MATH: \tan\alpha=1.25], where [MATH: \theta] and [MATH: \alpha] are acute angles measured in degrees, find [MATH: \theta+\alpha] in degrees to the nearest integer.
sections.readable_text: If [MATH: \cos\theta=0.64] and [MATH: \tan\alpha=1.25], where [MATH: \theta] and [MATH: \alpha] are acute angles measured in degrees, find [MATH: \theta+\alpha] in degrees to the nearest integer.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To find [MATH: \theta] and [MATH: \alpha] we use [MATH: \arccos] and [MATH: \arctan] respectively. We get

[MATH: \eqalign{ \cos\theta & = 0.64\ \arccos(\cos\theta) & = \arccos(0.64) \ \theta&=\arccos(0.64) }]

and

[MATH: \eqalign{ \tan\alpha & = 1.25 \ \arctan(\tan\alpha) & =\arctan(1.25) \ \alpha&=\arctan(1.25). }]

Then, using a calculator, we find [MATH: \eqalign{ \theta + \alpha & =\arccos(0.64)+\arctan(1.25)\ &=(50.208...)^{\circ} + (51.340...)^{\circ} \ & = (101.548...)^{\circ} \ & \approx 102^{\circ} }]

rounded to the nearest integer.

Watch out! If we round [MATH: \theta] and [MATH: \alpha] to the nearest integer, we get [MATH: \theta \approx 50^\circ] and [MATH: \alpha \approx 51^\circ.] After we sum up the angles we get an incorrect result: [MATH: θ + α|≈ 50^{∘} + 51^{∘} = 101^{∘}]

The correct answer is [MATH: 102^\circ,] not [MATH: 101^\circ.] This is a rounding error! To avoid this kind of error we have to round after we take the sum, not before.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To find [MATH: \theta] and [MATH: \alpha] we use [MATH: \arccos] and [MATH: \arctan] respectively. We get

\theta + \alpha & =\arccos(0.64)+\arctan(1.25)\

& = (101.548...)^{\circ}	\
& \approx 102^{\circ}

[MATH: θ + α|≈ 50^{∘} + 51^{∘} = 101^{∘}]

items.readable_text:
Content:
The inverse trigonometric functions are particularly useful when we need to find the measure of an angle in a right triangle.

Content:
To demonstrate, let's find the measure of the angle [MATH: \theta] indicated in the triangle below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/36de9546130017a8d8a4518676263c4e]

Content:
Since we are given the length of the hypotenuse and opposite sides to [MATH: \theta,] we can use sine to find the angle measurement. We have

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\sin (\theta) = \dfrac{\textrm{opposite}}{\textrm{hypotenuse}} &= \dfrac{5}{7}.
}]

Content:
We now calculate [MATH: \theta] using the inverse sine:

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\sin (\theta) &= \dfrac{5}{7}\[5pt]
\arcsin( \sin (\theta)) &= \arcsin\left(\dfrac{5}{7} \right)\[5pt]
\theta &= \arcsin\left(\dfrac{5}{7} \right)\[5pt]
&=(45.584\,6...)^\circ \[5pt]
&\approx 46^\circ
}]
rounded to the nearest integer.

\tan\alpha & = 1.25 \
\arctan(\tan\alpha) & =\arctan(1.25) \
\alpha&=\arctan(1.25).
}]

Then, using a calculator, we find
[MATH: \eqalign{
\theta + \alpha & =\arccos(0.64)+\arctan(1.25)\
&=(50.208...)^{\circ} + (51.340...)^{\circ} \
& = (101.548...)^{\circ}	\
& \approx 102^{\circ}
}]

rounded to the nearest integer.

Watch out! If we round [MATH: \theta] and [MATH: \alpha] to the nearest integer, we get [MATH: \theta \approx 50^\circ] and [MATH: \alpha \approx 51^\circ.] After we sum up the angles we get an incorrect result:
[MATH: θ + α|≈ 50^{∘} + 51^{∘} = 101^{∘}]

The correct answer is [MATH: 102^\circ,] not [MATH: 101^\circ.] This is a rounding error! To avoid this kind of error we have to round after we take the sum, not before.

Item 9 — Tutorial: Finding the Measure of an Angle in a Right Triangle Using Trigonometry

Content:
The inverse trigonometric functions are particularly useful when we need to find the measure of an angle in a right triangle.

Content:
To demonstrate, let's find the measure of the angle [MATH: \theta] indicated in the triangle below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/36de9546130017a8d8a4518676263c4e]

Content:
Since we are given the length of the hypotenuse and opposite sides to [MATH: \theta,] we can use sine to find the angle measurement. We have

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\sin (\theta) = \dfrac{\textrm{opposite}}{\textrm{hypotenuse}} &= \dfrac{5}{7}.
}]

Content:
We now calculate [MATH: \theta] using the inverse sine:

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\sin (\theta) &= \dfrac{5}{7}\[5pt]
\arcsin( \sin (\theta)) &= \arcsin\left(\dfrac{5}{7} \right)\[5pt]
\theta &= \arcsin\left(\dfrac{5}{7} \right)\[5pt]
&=(45.584\,6...)^\circ \[5pt]
&\approx 46^\circ
}]
rounded to the nearest integer.

Item 10 — Example: Finding the Measure of an Angle Given the Lengths of Two Sides of a Right Triangle

Example Prompt:
In a right triangle [MATH: \triangle ABC,] we have [MATH: AC = 9,] [MATH: BC=13,] and [MATH: m\angle A = \alpha.] Given that [MATH: \overline{AB}] is the hypotenuse of the triangle, find the value of [MATH: \alpha] (rounded to one decimal place).

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's sketch the triangle that's described.

[IMG: /graphics/653fd441b3decaa108994035e8d101eb]

Since we are given the lengths of the adjacent and opposite sides, we can use tangent to find the angle measurement. We have

[MATH: \tan \alpha= \dfrac{\textrm{opposite}}{\textrm{adjacent}} = \dfrac{13}{9}.]

We now calculate [MATH: \alpha] using the inverse tangent:

[MATH: \eqalign{
\tan \alpha &= \dfrac{13}{9}\[5pt]
\arctan( \tan \alpha) &= \arctan\left(\dfrac{13}{9} \right)\[5pt]
\alpha &= \arctan\left(\dfrac{13}{9} \right)\[5pt]
&=(55.304\,8...)^\circ\[5pt]
&\approx 55.3^\circ
}]
rounded to one decimal place.
